title: A wonder its teacher
theme: Many never hear of the self, and many who hear do not know it; its teacher and its knower are rare.

words.role: subject of the first relative clause (the self)
verb of the second relative clause
objective genitive with वक्ता and लब्धा

sandhi.type: savarṇa-dīrgha; visarga as r; aḥ before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: śravaṇāya + api: a + a give ā, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः). bahubhiḥ before y: after a vowel other than a or ā the visarga shows as r before a voiced sound. yaḥ before n: P. 6.1.114 (हशि च), P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः).

sandhi.type: aḥ before a; aḥ before a voiced consonant; final m
sandhi.rule: śṛṇvantaḥ + api: P. 6.1.113 (अतो रोरप्लुतादप्लुते), P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः), P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति). bahavaḥ before y: P. 6.1.114 (हशि च). yam before n: P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).

sandhi.type: aḥ before a voiced consonant; aḥ before a
sandhi.rule: āścaryaḥ before v: P. 6.1.114 (हशि च), P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः). kuśalaḥ + asya: P. 6.1.113 (अतो रोरप्लुतादप्लुते), P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति).
Normally ā + ā fuse into ā, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः); here the text keeps them apart at the end of a pāda (see the junction below).

sandhi_exceptions.note: labdhā āścaryaḥ: ā before ā is not fused. The words stand at the end of the third and the start of the fourth pāda, and both syllables are counted (11 + 11); fused, the half-line would have 21. Śaṅkara, quoting the verse in his Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya (3.4.51), writes them joined: लब्धाऽऽश्चर्यो.

samasa.meaning: taught by a skilled [teacher]; Śaṅkara: «कुशलेन निपुणेनाचार्येणानुशिष्टः»

morphology.note: Gerundive of labh, with -ya after a root ending in a labial with short a before it, P. 3.1.98 (पोरदुपधात्‌): ‘to be had’.

Optative third plural of vid ‘know’ (second class): vid-yā- with -us for the plural ending, P. 3.4.108 (झेर्जुस्), the ā dropped before it: vidyuḥ. Śaṅkara glosses it both as a present, «न विदन्ति», and as an optative, «न विजानीयुः».
vaktṛ, ‘speaker’, an agent noun in -tṛ, P. 3.1.133 (ण्वुल्तृचौ); so too labdhṛ ‘obtainer’ and jñātṛ ‘knower’.
āścarya ‘a marvel’, used here of persons: a speaker or knower of the self is a wonder, that is, rare. Raṅgarāmānuja: «दुर्लभः इत्यर्थः».

translation.literal: ‘[That] which is not obtainable even for hearing by many, which many, even hearing, would not know — a wonder [is] its speaker, skilled [is] its obtainer; a wonder [is] the knower taught by a skilled one.’
translation.readable: ‘Many never even get to hear of it; many who hear of it do not understand it. Rare is the one who can teach it, and gifted the one who receives it; rare is the one who knows it, having been taught by someone gifted.’

anvaya: यः बहुभिः श्रवणाय अपि न लभ्यः, यम् बहवः शृण्वन्तः अपि न विद्युः, अस्य वक्ता आश्चर्यः, लब्धा कुशलः, कुशलानुशिष्टः ज्ञाता आश्चर्यः ।
syntax: Two relative clauses with yaḥ and yam describe the self without naming it; the main clauses answer with asya, ‘of it’, and three nominal sentences in which agent nouns are the subjects: its speaker is a wonder, its obtainer skilled, the knower taught by a skilled one a wonder. The copula is understood throughout.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara takes kuśalaḥ with labdhā: the one who, having heard, attains it is skilled and one among many, «कुशलः निपुण एवानेकेषु लब्धा कश्चिदेव भवति». Raṅgarāmānuja makes both the teacher and the obtainer skilled, and both rare: «कुशलः प्राप्ता च, दुर्लभः इत्यर्थः».

Madhva’s text adds asya to the first word-group, ‘a wonder is its speaker’ (corrections.json), which makes the third pāda 12 syllables. The base has asya only once, with labdhā; Śaṅkara’s gloss, «अस्य वक्तापि आश्चर्यः», shows he took that asya with vaktā as well.

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: The halves count 23 and 22. The first pāda, śravaṇāyāpi bahubhir yo na labhyaḥ, has 12; the rest have 11. The hiatus labdhā āścaryaḥ at the pāda boundary is counted as written.

beginner: Death now explains why so few people know what Naciketas has asked about. Most never even hear of it. Of those who hear, many do not understand. Someone able to teach it is a rare thing, almost a wonder; so is someone able to take it in. And a person who truly knows it, because a capable teacher taught him, is rarer still. This is not said to discourage the boy. It is said to show how unusual his position is: he has asked the question, he is standing before a teacher who knows the answer, and he has proved that he is ready to listen. Three rare things have come together in one place, and the teaching depends on all three.
analogy: Like a rare piece of music: few have heard it, fewer understand it, and both a performer who can play it and a listener who can follow it are uncommon.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That the self is something many never hear of and many, hearing, do not understand; that its teacher and its learner are rare and gifted; and that a knower taught by a gifted teacher is a wonder.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: because most people are like those just described, and only one in thousands who seek the good comes to know the self, as Naciketas has: «यस्तु श्रेयोर्थी स सहस्रेषु कश्चिदेवात्मविद्भवति त्वद्विधः». Those who do not know it are the unfortunate, the unprepared: «अभागिनः असंस्कृतात्मानो न विजानीयुः».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: That even hearing of the supreme self is the fruit of great merit, «श्रवणलाभोऽपि महासुकृतफलमिति भावः», and that among those who hear, understanding is not easy: «न हि श्रोतृणां सर्वेषाम्, परमात्मप्रतिपत्तिः सुलभेति भावः».

commentary.q: Where else is the verse used?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: The Gītā echoes it closely (BG 2.29): one sees it as a wonder, another speaks of it as a wonder, and even having heard, no one knows it. Śaṅkara quotes the Kaṭha verse in his Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya (3.4.51) as scripture showing how hard the self is to know: «श्रुतिः दुर्बोधत्वमात्मनो दर्शयति».

advaita.text: The self is known only by a rare pupil taught by a skilled teacher: «आश्चर्यः ज्ञाता कश्चिदेव कुशलानुशिष्टः कुशलेन निपुणेनाचार्येणानुशिष्टः सन्».

visistadvaita.text: The subject is the supreme self, «यः प्रसिद्धः परमात्मा», which many cannot even hear of; a skilled teacher and a skilled obtainer are both rare.

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara takes the subject as the self (ātman), Raṅgarāmānuja as the supreme self (paramātman); both agree on the rarity of teacher and pupil. Madhva comments on the passage 1.2.4–8 only at 1.2.8.

parallels.note: The Gītā takes up the Kaṭha’s words: one sees it as a wonder, another speaks of it as a wonder, another hears of it as a wonder, and having heard, no one knows it.
‘Among thousands of people, one strives for perfection.’ Śaṅkara’s comment on the Kaṭha verse uses the same measure: «स सहस्रेषु कश्चिदेवात्मविद्भवति».

parallels.quote: श्रवणायापि बहुभिर्यो न लभ्यः शृण्वन्तोऽपि बहवो यं न विद्युः
parallels.note: Śaṅkara quotes the whole verse in the Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya to show that knowledge may arise only after obstacles are worn away, even in a later life.

contemporary.text: Anyone who has learned a demanding craft knows the verse’s three rarities: the chance to hear of it at all, a teacher who can really pass it on, and a learner able to receive it. When the three meet, something is transmitted that books alone do not carry. The verse asks the student to value the meeting, not only the information. This is a reflection, not part of the commentaries.

reflect.beginner: Who taught you something that you could not have learned alone?
reflect.deeper: Why should both teaching and learning this be called ‘a wonder’?
reflect.practice: Thank, in words or in writing, one teacher whose teaching you now carry.
